title: Leaders Who Empower a Surrogate to Speak for Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article warns senior leaders about lieutenants and project leaders who invoke the senior leader's name and authority to force compliance rather than leading in their own right. The piece distinguishes effective delegation -- where trusted colleagues perform the actual functions of leadership -- from surrogate leadership, where a lieutenant borrows authority to make demands feel non-negotiable. The author argues this tactic backfires, breeding obedience instead of engagement and eroding the credibility of both the lieutenant and the senior leader they cite.
points: Effective delegation requires trusted lieutenants to actually perform leadership functions, not just relay a senior leader's mandates.
Citing a senior leader's authority to force execution elevates short-term compliance but kills candid discussion, innovation, and risk-taking.
Team members quickly recognize a leader who speaks 'under the banner' of someone else as a puppet rather than a real leader.
The senior leader often has no idea a lieutenant is leading this way -- and it isn't hard for them to find out once they look.
quotes: What they don’t do is act as a surrogate for the senior leader.
When lieutenants drive projects forward by speaking for the senior leader, using their name to create mandates and demanding execution by citing them, they can create a mess.
Framing decisions as coming from above and citing that authority to justify instructions can elevate compliance but diminish engagement.
Unfortunately, name-dropping the senior leader stifles candid discussion, innovation, and risk-taking. People quickly view the lieutenant as a puppet — a leader unworthy of respect.
Ironically, the more a leader cites authority, the less authority they actually have.
